```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  eval = TRUE,
  fig.width = 6,
  fig.height = 4
)
library(flexyBayes)
set.seed(1)
```

A *surrogate* (or emulator) replaces an expensive simulator with a fast map
from parameter sets to outputs. The flexyBayes surrogate (contract C7) does
one extra thing that an ordinary regression emulator does not: it reports a
predictive **distribution**, not a point. Reporting the predictive standard
deviation alongside the mean is what lets a downstream calibration or inverse
step stay honest about emulator error instead of silently treating the
surrogate as exact.

This vignette walks the whole loop on a small, self-contained example -- ingest
an ensemble, fit a surrogate, read its predictive distribution, invert it against
observed data, and check whether it distorted the output distribution. The
reference surrogate ships with flexyBayes and needs no other package, so every
code chunk below runs as shown.

## A simulator we can check against

We use a linear forward model `y = G theta` so the truth is known and the
inversion is exact in expectation. Three outputs, two parameters, and a little
observation noise.

```{r ensemble}
g <- rbind(c(1.5, -0.8), c(0.4, 1.1), c(-0.9, 0.6)) # 3 outputs x 2 params
n_train <- 300L
theta <- cbind(
  p1 = runif(n_train, -3, 3),
  p2 = runif(n_train, -3, 3)
)
y <- theta %*% t(g) + matrix(rnorm(n_train * 3L, 0, 0.1), n_train, 3L)
colnames(y) <- c("o1", "o2", "o3")
```

The ensemble is ingested through the C5 contract, so any conforming producer
(a PESTO manifest, a raw `apsimx` run, a saved file) feeds a surrogate the same
way. Here we build one directly from the design and the outputs.

```{r fb-ensemble}
ens <- fb_ensemble(
  params = as.data.frame(theta),
  outputs = as.data.frame(y),
  provenance = list(source = "raw")
)
ens
```

## Fit a surrogate and read its distribution

`fit_surrogate()` trains the emulator. The default reference method, `"rff"`,
is a random-Fourier-features Bayesian linear model whose predictive variance is
set by evidence maximisation, so the reported standard deviation is calibrated
rather than an arbitrary ridge.

```{r fit}
sur <- fit_surrogate(ens)
sur
```

`predict()` returns, for each emulated output `<o>`, a `<o>_mean` and a
`<o>_sd` column. The standard deviation is the distribution-preserving part of
the contract.

```{r predict}
newdata <- data.frame(p1 = c(1.0, -2.0), p2 = c(0.5, 1.5))
predict(sur, newdata)
```

By default the reference surrogate fits the outputs **jointly**, so it preserves
the cross-output predictive covariance, not only the per-output marginals.
`predict(..., cov = TRUE)` returns that covariance as a per-row array, and
`fb_cov_slice()` reads one row's `k`-by-`k` slice.

```{r joint-cov}
pc <- predict(sur, newdata, cov = TRUE)
round(fb_cov_slice(pc, 1L), 3)
```

The diagonal of that slice equals the `<o>_sd` values squared, exactly -- the
marginal contract is never broken by the joint fit.

## Invert: recover parameters from data

`fb_surrogate_ies()` is the calibration consumer. It runs an Ensemble Smoother
with Multiple Data Assimilation (ES-MDA), driving a prior parameter ensemble
toward agreement with observed data using only the surrogate in place of the
simulator. Because the surrogate is distribution-preserving, its predictive
variance is folded into the data covariance, so emulator uncertainty inflates
the assimilation noise where the emulator is least sure.

```{r invert}
theta_true <- c(p1 = 1.2, p2 = -0.7)
observed <- as.numeric(g %*% theta_true)
names(observed) <- c("o1", "o2", "o3")

prior <- data.frame(
  p1 = rnorm(300, 0, 1.5),
  p2 = rnorm(300, 0, 1.5)
)
fit <- fb_surrogate_ies(sur, observed, obs_sd = 0.05, prior = prior, seed = 7)
fit
```

The posterior ensemble concentrates near the truth, and the data misfit falls
from prior to posterior.

```{r invert-recovery}
rbind(
  truth = theta_true,
  prior_mean = colMeans(prior),
  posterior_mean = colMeans(fit$posterior)
)
```

## Check: did the surrogate distort the distribution?

A surrogate can recover the mean while getting the *spread* or the *cross-output
correlation* wrong. `fb_surrogate_ppc()` tests the predictive distribution
itself, by drawing from the surrogate at held-out parameter sets and comparing
the draw cloud to the true simulator outputs with kernR's maximum-mean-discrepancy
posterior-predictive check. The MMD test lives in kernR -- flexyBayes only
generates the predictive sample -- so this chunk runs only when kernR is
installed.

```{r ppc, eval = requireNamespace("kernR", quietly = TRUE)}
set.seed(4)
held <- data.frame(p1 = runif(60, -2.5, 2.5), p2 = runif(60, -2.5, 2.5))
truth_held <- held$p1 %o% g[, 1] + held$p2 %o% g[, 2] +
  matrix(rnorm(60 * 3L, 0, 0.1), 60, 3L)
colnames(truth_held) <- c("o1", "o2", "o3")

check <- fb_surrogate_ppc(
  sur, held, as.data.frame(truth_held),
  n_draws = 5L, seed = 1L, n_permutations = 199L
)
c(p_value = check$p_value, reject = check$reject)
```

A high p-value (no rejection) means the surrogate's predictive draws are
indistinguishable from the simulator's outputs -- the distribution was preserved,
not merely the mean. The check is joint by default, so it exercises the
cross-output correlation, not only each output's spread.

## Many outputs: a low-rank covariance

When a simulator has a large number of outputs whose covariance is driven by a
few latent factors, the dense `k`-by-`k` covariance is wasteful. `cov_rank = q`
stores the cross-output covariance in a rank-`q` factor-analysis form, reducing
the storage from order `k` squared to order `k` times `q`, while reproducing the
covariance diagonal -- and hence every `<o>_sd` -- exactly.

```{r lowrank}
sur_lr <- fit_surrogate(ens, cov_rank = 1L)
sur_lr$fit$sigma_lr$rank
```

Both consumers use the factored form natively, so the dense covariance is never
formed: `fb_surrogate_ies()` folds it into the Kalman update through the Woodbury
identity, and `fb_surrogate_ppc()` samples it factored (and, with
`project = TRUE`, runs the discrepancy test in the `q`-dimensional factor space,
which is cheaper and higher-powered on the correlated structure for a large
output count). The factor itself is fitted by an eigen-truncation,
factor-analysis EM (`cov_method = "fa"`, more faithful when the residual noise is
uneven across outputs), or `"auto"`.

## Where the seam goes

The reference `rff` surrogate keeps flexyBayes standalone-functional. Richer
emulators -- a Gaussian process, a conditional mean embedding -- register through
`register_surrogate()` and are consumed through exactly the same `predict()`
contract, so the inversion and the check above work unchanged with a sibling's
surrogate in place of the reference. The contract is the interface, not any one
implementation.

A surrogate is only as trustworthy as its predictive distribution. The point of
making the standard deviation a contract requirement, and of shipping the
inversion and the predictive check alongside the emulator, is that the
distribution can be inspected and falsified rather than assumed. The reference
surrogate is deliberately simple, so for a stiff or sharply non-linear simulator
a richer registered emulator will preserve the distribution where the reference
cannot, and the same predictive check is what tells the two apart.
```
